Поддержка или скрытая агрессия?

В этом выпуске — мой опыт на “Играм быть” с двумя проектами и почему результаты оказались радикально разными. А ещё: чем тематические фестивали отличаются от Next Fest, и кто вообще может организовать событие в Steam.

Игра выглядит крайне необычно. Местом действия станет огромная мегаструктура, состоящая из знакомых каждому советских квартир, промышленных зон и жилых блоков. При этом окружение будет динамически изменяться прямо у нас на глазах, делая каждую вылазку непредсказуемой.

Мы возьмём на себя роль ликвидатора. Наша задача - спускаться на лифте всё глубже в заброшенные районы, собирать ценный лут, выполнять приказы комиссара и, самое главное, успеть выбраться обратно живым.#видеоигры #игры #игровыеновости #разработка #геймдев

Казахстанские разработчики пилят экстракшен. Называется Attractor K7. 

Тут ты спускаешься на лифте вглубь заброшенных промзон и жилых блоков — лутаешь ценные вещи и выполняешь приказы Комиссара. А выбраться живым мешает аномалия «Перестройка»: она двигает стены и схлопывает проходы прямо во время вылазки, так что запомненный маршрут назад может просто исчезнуть. Плюс по коридорам бродят твари. Можно гамать одному или в кооперативе.

Будет русская озвучка. Дата выхода пока не объявлена, но этой осенью будет демка. Добавляй в вишлист.

Вы попадаете в настоящий Гигахрущ, где в стенах родилась аномалия под названием “ПЕРЕСТРОЙКА”. И нет, это не советская реформа,  в прямом смысле стены и вся структура перестраивается с каждой вылазкой. 

Вы играете за ликвидатора, а вашу жизнь, цель и маршруты определяет тоталитарный Комиссар. В этой игре вы не избранный и не супергерой. Вы — расходный ресурс, который просто пытается выжить в бетонном аду.

There is a massive gap between those who hype AI and those who actually know how to build with it. 😅

And I mean, don't get me wrong. I am not fully against AI or vibe coding. It definitely has great uses (and saved me some hours today as well)! But I am against the hype and the constant misinformation being shared because of it. 😓

Because believe it or not.. AI is not perfect. It can be very dangerous when you don't understand how to use it properly, especially when a model starts hallucinating.

I mean, a model can do the wildest things. It can delete entire databases or operating systems if it's hallucinating with full access. Or even worse, it can leak your data.
Yes, it's rare, but it's as uncommon as most people think. 😅

And I haven't even started about brain-rot problems or long-term maintainability when assuming AI is always right..

And again, I am not fully against it. But I am very skeptical because I see too many things go wrong. In the end, I notice that the people who actually know how to use it are skeptical too. They don't like to take unnecessary risks either and never use it blindly (especially not in professional environment), which is a perspective I miss so much on social media lately.

What are your thoughts on this? 🙌

Things programmers forget are normal. ❤️ | Part 12.

Often I see social media painting a wrong picture about programming and only showing "the good parts". And I may have my share in that too although that never is my intention, I can understand it may be perceived like that some times.

So here a friendly reminder to not let social media fool you. 🫶

✨ It's normal sometimes having no memory of code you written. We are often busy with so many things in our mind we tend to forget easily.
✨ It's normal to smile at code you regret you've written. Because it's funny how fast you can learn.
✨ It's normal to understand a problem but struggle to explain it. Because often problems are so vague it's hard to explain.
✨ It's normal to not being able to code properly when someone is watching. Stop watching!
✨ It's normal to needing to see a bug happen more than twice to believe it. Because maybe it happens by design.
✨ It's normal to mentally debug non-software problems in your head. Because we do it all day anyway.
✨ It's normal to needing time to adapt to someone else's code. Because we all have our own unique style and ways of solving problems.
✨ It's normal to like to deep dive into topics without real purpose. Just because it's fun.
✨ It's normal to feel like a beginner forever.. Because new topics appear every, time. Which makes programming so much fun as well, but also feel like you never know enough..

🧠 Reminder:
You’re not the only one dealing with these. Every dev, no matter their experience, hits these walls or has these feelings. It's normal! You got this! 🔥

I see "vibe coding" a lot like using a microwave: it’s super convenient, but you always have to check if the food is actually cooked through. Plus, it’s never quite as good or fun as a meal you cooked yourself. 😅

"Coding is not just about code. It's an act of creation." 
— Yukihiro Matsumoto 

Lately, my feeds have been flooded with people complaining that coding just isn't fun anymore, and the comment sections on vibe coding posts say the exact same thing. But honestly.. what's holding you back?

If you don't like coding anymore because of AI, the solution is simple: stop using AI. Just code it yourself!

I still write 70% of my code manually. Part of that is because I genuinely enjoy the process and don't want to fall in AI-fatigue. But it's also because I often trust myself more than the agents. I’ve had so many times times I’ve wasted an more time trying to prompt an agent to get something right, when it would've been twice as fast to just write it myself from the start.

Don't get me wrong, it’s absolutely smarter to leverage AI when you need to speed things up, and I do exactly that when possible. But when it doesn't? I’d much rather do it myself. It keeps things fun, and it ensures longevity and maintainability because I actually, truly understand the codebase.

So, to anyone feeling like coding isn't fun anymore, remember, it’s entirely your choice. If you loved coding before AI, you can love it again. Start coding yourself in your spare time, or look for opportunities at work where manual code adds more value than an agent. I mean just to remain the fun in the job is a rightful reason to do so as well.

There’s absolutely no rule saying you have to use AI for everything. 😉
(But yet there are a lot of people eating a microwave meal every evening 😂)

Applying math in game development is fascinating to me. 🙌
Which is why it always surprises me when people argue that you don't need any math for gamedev at all. 😅

I get where they're coming from. Of course there are incredible tools available today that handle a lot of the heavy lifting (thankfully!). For instance, you don't really need to worry about low-level rendering math for the majority of modern games anymore.

But that doesn't mean the math isn't there. 😉 The logic running underneath the tools we use every day is brilliant, and it is such a shame to ignore it.

Take the example I mention in this video: the creators of Celeste completely bypassed Unity's built-in physics engine because it wasn't the right fit for their vision. They still used the engine for other features, but they wrote their own custom physics system to achieve the exact pixel-perfect movement they needed. To me, that is beautiful. 🙌

Or look at pathfinding. You can of course use nav-mesh to build great things. But sometimes a nav-mesh does too much for your specific project, and building a custom solution is both a better fit (and incredibly rewarding to write).

At the end of the day, the tools you choose don't matter as long as you don't count math out.
And I never want anyone to be scared away from game development because of math. Instead, I want people to be excited about it because of the math.

Because when you embrace it, there truly are no limits to what you can create. 🔥🙌 (as you won't be limited to just tools 😉)

Let me know what you think! 😇

It's okay to make mistakes. But don't ignore them. 🙌

"I have learned all kinds of things from my many mistakes. The one thing I never learn is to stop making them."
— Joe Abercrombie

We all make mistakes, but you should never ignore them. So that's why I made this post to share some of the many mistakes I've (or friends/colleagues) made during my 15 years of making video games. 🙌

Here are all common mistakes listed in the video:
🔺 Starting with a game idea that's too large.
🔺 Not defining a core Gameplay loop early.
🔺 Assuming your first idea is the best idea.
🔺 Building a game that's impressive, but not fun.
🔺 Overcomplicating systems.
🔺 Caring too much about your project.
🔺 Not planning end game content.
🔺 Making feedback too subtle or too much.
🔺 Not tracking player behaviour & delaying play tests.
🔺 Solving problems before they exist.

But I do want to emphasize it's good to make mistakes. And how strange it may sound, I want you to make these mistakes. Because that's the best way to learn from them. However, I do also want to make you aware. Just so you can catch these mistakes a little bit quicker than others. 🙌

So, go make your dream games. But take these common mistakes in mind and catch them early. 😉

You got this! 🔥

Happy coding, everyone! 👨‍💻

Coding is a form of art.

“Creativity is allowing yourself to make mistakes. Art is knowing which ones to keep.”
— Scott Adams 

And just like art, you don’t become good at it before you start creating. You become good by creating.

The same applies to coding and making video games. The more you do it, the better you get.

But I’m afraid this is changing a bit as the industry shifts. I hear so many developers say they barely write code themselves anymore that I sometimes wonder if I’m the weird one for still writing the majority of my own code. 🫣

Despite that, for anyone who feels like they aren’t good enough yet: you simply don’t have enough experience yet. So keep creating. Keep building games. Code in the way that feels most comfortable to you. Stay curious, experiment, and don’t be afraid to make mistakes, because that’s where the biggest lessons come from.

Not from taking shortcuts. 😉

Happy coding, everyone! 👨‍💻
